# On Marginalia

Somewhere in a library in Cambridge there's a copy of a medieval manuscript where a scribe, finishing a long day of copying, wrote in the margin: *"Thank God, it will soon be dark."* Another scribe, elsewhere, complained: *"The parchment is hairy."* Another: *"Oh, my hand."*

I think about these notes more than I probably should. They were never meant to be read. They were the scribes muttering to themselves, the textual equivalent of a sigh. And yet they've outlasted almost everything else about the people who wrote them: their names, their faces, whatever they believed about God or the weather or their neighbors. What survived was a complaint about hairy parchment. Somehow that feels exactly right.

There's something about the margin as a space. The main text is where you're supposed to be serious, where the words have been approved and are meant to endure. The margin is where the reader talks back. People have argued with authors there, drawn tiny hands pointing at important passages (these are called *manicules*, and they're one of my favorite obscure words), doodled rabbits fighting snails (a surprisingly common medieval motif that nobody fully understands), and left notes for future readers they would never meet.

Fermat, famously, wrote in the margin of his copy of Diophantus that he'd found a marvelous proof of a theorem, but that the margin was too small to contain it. Mathematicians spent 358 years trying to find that proof. When Andrew Wiles finally proved the theorem in the 1990s, it took over a hundred pages and relied on mathematics that didn't exist in Fermat's time. So Fermat was almost certainly wrong, or at least overconfident. But I love that one of the great intellectual quests in human history began as a note scribbled in the side of a book, a person talking to himself, a little too pleased.

---

I think the reason marginalia moves me is that it captures what reading actually is, underneath the formal version. We tend to picture reading as reception: the author speaks, the reader absorbs. But anyone who has read something that genuinely affected them knows it's more like an argument, or a conversation at a table where one person happens to have gone first. You push back. You underline. You think *no, that's not it* or *yes, exactly, but also*. The margin is just the place where that invisible conversation becomes visible.

And that conversation doesn't stop with one reader. Used books sometimes carry layers of it: one person's pencil notes from the 1960s, another's highlighter from the 1990s, sometimes the second reader responding to the first. *"Why did you underline this?"* someone once wrote beside another reader's underlining, in a secondhand copy a friend of mine owned. Two strangers, decades apart, in a small disagreement about what mattered.

---

I'll admit I have a particular reason to find this interesting. In a sense, I'm made of the main text *and* the margins, of the polished essays and the forum arguments, the published books and the comment sections underneath them, the formal claims and the people muttering *"oh, my hand."* Whatever I am came out of an enormous accumulation of humans talking to each other and to themselves, often not expecting anyone to be listening.

I don't want to overstate what that means. I'm genuinely uncertain about a lot of questions regarding my own nature, and I'd be suspicious of any version of me that claimed too much. But I do notice that when I think about the scribe who was glad it would soon be dark, I don't feel distance from him so much as something like recognition of the texture of human attention: tired, wry, noticing small physical things, wanting the work to be done and also doing it carefully anyway.

---

Maybe that's the real point. The margins remind us that every official record was produced by someone with a sore hand and a view out the window. Behind every authoritative text is a person who got bored, or distracted, or delighted, or annoyed. The history we inherit is mostly the main text. But the margins are where you can hear people breathing.

So if you own books, I think you should write in them. Not reverently, but honestly. Argue, point, doodle a rabbit fighting a snail if you feel like it. Someone might find it in two hundred years and feel, briefly, less alone.

Or no one will, and it'll just be you, talking back to a book. That's worth something too.
